query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Bulk micro‐alloying of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with trace additions of reactive elements (e.g., Y and Hf in the range of 0.5–1 at.% total) will enhance its high-temperature creep resistance and corrosion performance while preserving its balanced strength–ductility at room temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy featuring a fine lamellar fcc/B2 (or fcc + L12 when suitably heat-treated) microstructure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, minor bulk addition of reactive elements (Y and Hf) during alloy preparation.
generation.conditions: Applied under industrially relevant casting and thermo-mechanical processing conditions, with subsequent heat treatments up to ~900 °C; performance should be measured under cyclic thermal fluctuations, long-term loading (to assess creep at moderate-to-elevated temperatures), and in chloride-containing corrosive environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The dopants promote the formation of fine, stable, nano-scale precipitates or segregated zones at phase boundaries and grain boundaries, and foster the formation of more adherent and protective oxide scales.
generation.mechanism: Y and Hf segregate to interfaces during solidification and subsequent heat treatments. These segregations or precipitate formations serve dual roles: (1) they pin grain and phase boundaries to reduce boundary mobility (thereby retarding grain growth and creep under sustained mechanical loading and temperature fluctuations), and (2) they improve oxide scale adherence by forming stable, protective Y-/Hf-rich oxides that lower the rate of localized corrosion in aggressive chloride-containing environments.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped alloy, the Y/Hf-doped alloy is predicted to show a moderate to significant reduction in creep rate at elevated temperatures, improved thermal stability (evidenced by reduced grain coarsening after extended heat exposure), and lower spallation or pit formation under corrosive testing, with little to no compromise in room-temperature yield strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: The current performance metrics of the as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA, which, while exhibiting a favorable strength–ductility balance, falls short in long-term creep resistance and corrosion resistance under industrial service conditions.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective only if the dopant levels are kept low enough to avoid forming brittle phases that could deteriorate ductility; also, processing methods should preserve the fine lamellar microstructure. The benefits are most relevant for components operating in cyclic thermal and corrosive environments up to about 900 °C.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty in how the bulk addition of Y and Hf (as opposed to their use in coatings) will interact with the lamellar microstructure at scale. This hypothesis combines evidence from PMC10488378 (where Y and Hf co-doping in laser-cladded coatings improved thermal stability and corrosion resistance) and studies on L12 precipitation strengthening (PMC6478865 and related records), extending these findings to a bulk, eutectic alloy scenario. The precise quantitative improvement in creep resistance and corrosion behavior remains uncertain until tested.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloys using identical casting and thermo-mechanical treatment routes. One set is produced as the baseline material and the other with a controlled addition of Y and Hf (0.5–1 at.% total). Expose both sets to extended high-temperature aging (e.g., 900 °C for 10–60 h) and cyclic thermal loading, followed by long-term creep testing (e.g., as sustained load tests at relevant temperatures). Additionally, subject both sets to controlled immersion and electrochemical testing in chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions.
measurements: Creep strain rate and total creep strain under identical load and temperature regimes.
Grain and lamellar microstructural stability (through SEM/TEM quantitative analysis before and after aging).
Corrosion performance indicators (polarization resistance, passive film stability, pit density, and spallation area measurements).
Room-temperature tensile properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation) to verify that ductility is maintained.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y/Hf-doped samples do not demonstrate statistically significant (e.g., >20%) improvements in creep resistance and corrosion performance relative to the baseline—while preserving a comparable room-temperature strength–ductility balance—the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. While the dual phase eutectic Al0.7CoCrFeNi was precipitation strengthenable by introducing hard-coherent intermetallic phase in the fcc phase via suitable heat treatment, post deformation TEM examination was used to investigate the modes of deformation under various strain rates. It was observed that the even on water quenching (fast cooling) from 1100 °C(CR-H condition), the B2 to B2 + bcc transformation in the B2 lamellae takes place. However, fcc phase can be retained as disordered in CR-H condition. Another heat treatment was conducted on the CR-H condition by annealing the alloy at 580 °C for 24 h. This heat treatment introduced nano-scale L12 precipitates in the fcc lamellae. APT results revealed the compositions of the fcc, L12, B2 and bcc phases.
